title: Genetic and Immunological Characterization of Patients with Suspected Inborn Errors of Immunity
summary:
Background: The immune system protects the body from pathogens. In congenital disorders of the immune system, genetic mutations cause the body’s own defenses to malfunction or become dysregulated. Affected individuals may suffer from recurrent or severe infections, chronic inflammation, allergies, or conditions in which the immune system turns against the body itself. Despite modern diagnostic methods, the cause remains unclear in many affected individuals.

Research Question: The goal of this study is to identify the genetic causes of congenital immune system disorders and to better understand their effects. In particular, the study aims to investigate how genetic changes are related to symptoms and the results of immunological tests. Furthermore, the study will examine whether genetic changes that are not yet fully understood influence the function of the immune system and contribute to the development of the disease.

Methodology: The study includes children, adolescents, and adults with suspected congenital immune system disorders. Medical information, disease histories, and existing test results are collected and evaluated. Blood samples are used to investigate genetic variations and to analyze the composition and function of immune cells and key immune processes. In certain cases, additional blood samples from the parents or a skin sample may be required. With appropriate consent, the collected samples and associated medical data may be stored for further scientific research. By integrating genetic, clinical, and immunological test results, the study aims to contribute to a better understanding of previously unexplained diseases and, in the long term, to improve diagnostic options and treatment for affected individuals.

interventions.name: This study is a non-interventional, clinical-translational observational study involving pediatric and adult patients with suspected inborn errors of immunity (IEI). Recruitment is conducted through the Clinic of Pediatric Immunology and Rheumatology at the Center for Pediatric and Adolescent Medici

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
The study will include pediatric and adult female patients with a clinical suspicion of an inborn error of immunity (IEI) based on the clinical criteria of the relevant S3 guideline. Patients must have been referred to the Clinic for Pediatric Immunology and Rheumatology at the Center for Pediatric and Adolescent Medicine at the University Hospital Bonn or presented for evaluation at the University Hospital Bonn’s interdisciplinary Immunoboard by the participating departments or collaborating clinics. Eligibility for participation in the study must have been confirmed by the responsible interdisciplinary team.
A prerequisite for participation in the study is written, informed consent to participate in the study as well as to the respective genetic, immunophenotypic, and functional tests. For minor patients, the required consents from legal guardians and—depending on age and capacity to consent—the consent of the affected children and adolescents must be obtained in accordance with the study protocol. The appropriate consents must be obtained for the collection and use of biological samples. If, in individual cases, a skin biopsy or a genetic test involving one parent (Duo analysis) or both parents (Rrio analysis) is planned, the necessary consents must also be obtained for these procedures.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients with no clinical evidence of an inborn error of immunity (IEI) will be excluded from participating in the study. Individuals from whom valid informed consent to participate in the study cannot be obtained due to insurmountable language or other communication barriers will also be excluded. A general refusal to participate in the study will also result in exclusion.
